title: Concurrent KV-cache eviction cascade postmortem
summary: A concurrent eviction cascade in the prefix/KV cache during a burst of long-running streaming requests caused latency spikes and client-facing 5xx errors in the Hosted API. The immediate trigger was a combination of an aggressive autoscaler decision and synchronous cache rehydration work on the serving threadpool.
content:
Executive summary:

On 2026-03-12 09:14 UTC we observed a global uptick in tail latency for the Hosted API streaming endpoint and a correlated rise in 5xx rates. The spike started as a region-local capacity shift in us-west1 and propagated to other regions as traffic routed and clients retried. Root cause: simultaneous eviction/rehydration activity on the in-memory KV/prefix cache when multiple model-serving processes were scaled up at once. Rehydration was synchronous and executed on the serving threadpool, which caused head-of-line blocking, thread starvation, and downstream timeouts in the streaming path. Compounding factors: (1) the autoscaler decision threshold parameter had been recently lowered for burst responsiveness (PR #1874) and resulted in more aggressive scale-ups, (2) circuit-breaker backpressure to the fallback tier was not applied early in the streaming path, and (3) monitoring and alerting thresholds for synchronous cache-backfill latency were too lax.

Impact:
- Duration: ~32 minutes (09:14 UTC to 09:46 UTC) of elevated errors and tail latency, with intermittent client retries extending perceived failure window to ~47 minutes in some regions.
- Affected customers: all Hosted API customers using streaming endpoints; ~18% experienced degraded responses (5xx or >3s tail latency) during the peak.
- User-visible: increased 5xx rate from baseline 0.06% to 4.2% at peak; p95 latency for streaming connect/first-chunk rose from ~140ms to ~2.4s.
- Internal: several autoscaler/placement adjustments happened concurrently, producing noisy capacity churn.

Timeline (UTC):
- 09:12 - Gradual increase in cold-started model instances reported by the monitoring dashboard (an earlier small traffic surge triggered scale-ups in us-west1).
- 09:14 - First pager: on-call SRE page for elevated Hosted API 5xx (pager escalated to L2).
- 09:16 - Investigation: high queue lengths on serving threadpool, spike in synchronous rehydration operations (logs show KVCache::rehydrate calls on request-path threads).
- 09:19 - Engineers experimentally reduced new-instance weight in loadbalancer to limit immediate impact; no immediate reduction in 5xx.
- 09:22 - Temporary mitigation: disabled synchronous cache rehydrate on request threads (switched to background async rehydrate) via emergency flag in orchestrator. Error rate started dropping after 6 minutes.
- 09:28 - Autoscaler cooldown increased and aggressive scale-down rules temporarily disabled to stop oscillation.
- 09:38 - Error rate returned near baseline; continued monitoring for residual retries and client-side backoff issues.
- 09:46 - Incident declared resolved for customer-impacting errors; follow-up tasks assigned.

Root cause analysis:
Primary cause: synchronous KV-cache rehydration executed on the serving request threadpool during large concurrent scale-ups. The code path is: when an instance receives a request for a prefix not present in memory, the handler calls KVCache::rehydrate synchronously before continuing request processing. Under a large number of near-simultaneous new instances (driven by autoscaler), many of these rehydrate calls occur at the same time and run on the shared serving threadpool. Rehydration is I/O and CPU intensive (deserializing large prefix blobs, warming local L1 caches, and deserialization of chunked embeddings), which blocked other streaming request handling and caused timeouts upstream.

Contributing factors:
- Autoscaler tuning change (merged in runtime PR #1874) reduced the target CPU threshold and increased targetProvision rate to minimize cold-start latency. During this burst it produced several dozen new instances in a short window.
- No circuit-breaker/backpressure early in streaming handshake: streaming connect path allowed requests to queue to blocked threads rather than fail fast to allow graceful fallback to non-streaming endpoints.
- Observability gap: we lacked a high-fidelity metric for concurrent rehydrate operations per node; existing metric only tracked aggregate cache hits/misses and client-side retries, which delayed root-cause identification.
- Runbook gap: the runbook for "High tail latency / streaming 5xx" did not include steps to check for synchronous cache-work on serving threads nor a clear emergency toggle to enforce async-only rehydrate behavior.

Detection and response effectiveness:
- Pager triggered within 2 minutes of the increase; SRE rotation and L2 engaged promptly.
- Runbook partially useful (generic latency troubleshooting) but required ad-hoc debugging to discover synchronous rehydrate.
- The emergency flag to switch rehydrate to background worker existed but did not have a documented safe toggle procedure for the Hosted API cluster; this slowed mitigation by ~3 minutes.

Immediate mitigations (what we did to stop customer impact):
1) Flip emergency flag to make KVCache::rehydrate asynchronous and bound to a background worker pool with a small concurrency cap. This prevented serving threads from being blocked by rehydration work.
2) Increase autoscaler cooldown and temporarily reduce scale-up aggressiveness to prevent more simultaneous instance launches while cache warmed.
3) Route new traffic to warmed instances where possible (LB weight adjustments) and enable temporary rate-limiting to high-retry clients.
4) Monitor in real-time (logs and metrics) for rehydration backlog and threadpool saturation until stable.

Post-incident corrective actions (short-term):
- Safety patch: make rehydrate on-request path async by default and add a feature flag so we can toggle back in controlled experiments. (owner: runtime team, PR submitted: #1881, target: 2026-03-18)
- Observability: add metric concurrent_kv_rehydrate_count per instance + alert when > 5 for > 1m. (owner: observability, target: 2026-03-16)
- Runbook updates: add explicit checks for synchronous cache work, include instructions to flip the emergency async flag, and add LB weight adjustment steps. (owner: eng-sre, target: 2026-03-15)
- Autoscaler tuning rollback: revert aggressive scale-up parameter change and add canary rollout for any autoscaler tuning. (owner: platform-engineering, target: 2026-03-17)

Longer-term mitigations (roadmap items):
- Architect cache warmup: implement proactive background prewarming for popular prefixes on instance startup to avoid on-request rehydrate storms. (quarter roadmap Q2 2026)
- Backpressure: implement early-fail fast path in streaming handshake so requests can fallback to non-stream streaming behavior or queue on a separate buffered worker pool. (owner: serving-runtime, Q2 2026)
- Autoscaler safety: implement burst-detection logic that staggers scale-ups across placement groups rather than launching many instances simultaneously. (owner: platform, Q3 2026)
- Chaos/Load-testing: extend chaos tests to include concurrent cold-start+cache-eviction scenarios and validate the async rehydrate safety. (owner: SRE/qa, Q2 2026)

Draft runbook additions (for "High tail latency or streaming 5xx"):
1) Immediate triage:
   - Confirm global/regional impact via Hosted API dashboards and error-rate graphs.
   - Check serving-threadpool utilization and queue lengths (metric: serving_threadpool_queue_len).
   - Inspect metric concurrent_kv_rehydrate_count per instance (if not present, inspect logs for KVCache::rehydrate entries).
2) If concurrent rehydrate activity > threshold:
   - Flip \"rehydrate_async_mode\" emergency flag to ON for affected pool(s).
   - If no emergency flag exists, temporarily set process-level env var to force background rehydration and restart one instance for verification before rolling change.
3) Autoscaler actions:
   - Increase scale-up cooldown to 300s and reduce targetProvision rate by 50% for the affected region.
   - Pause any rollout of autoscaler tuning until safe.
4) Traffic shaping:
   - Adjust LB weights to favor warmed instances and route new traffic away from recently scaled nodes.
   - Apply temporary client-level rate limits for high-retry clients.
5) Post-mitigation validation:
   - Monitor p95/p99 latency, 5xx rate, and rehydrate backlog for 30 minutes.
   - Run synthetic streaming requests to validate stability.

Lessons learned:
- Avoid synchronous heavy work on request-serving threads; heavy warmup/load tasks must be delegated to background workers with bounded concurrency.
- Autoscaler changes need safe canary windows and staggered placement to avoid synchronized cold-start work across many nodes.
- Runbooks must include service-specific failure modes (e.g., cache rehydration) that are easy to search and include exact emergency toggling steps.
- Observability matters: create per-instance concurrency metrics early to shorten MTTI.

Action items (owners and deadlines):
- runtime: land async rehydrate default + feature flag + unit/integration tests (owner: Priya Desai, due 2026-03-18)
- observability: emit concurrent_kv_rehydrate_count, alert, dashboard (owner: Marisol Vega, due 2026-03-16)
- eng-sre: update runbook, add playbook checklist, and schedule a runbook drill (owner: Aisha Kaur, due 2026-03-15)
- platform-engineering: revert scale-up tuning, implement staged scale-up plan, add canary gating for autoscaler PRs (owner: Liam O'Connor, due 2026-03-17)
- qa/sre: create chaos test case for concurrent cold-start + cache rehydrate (owner: Benji Morales, due 2026-04-01)

Appendix - on-call raw notes (verbatim):
- 09:15 (Benji): seeing KVCache::rehydrate spikes in logs across 6 nodes in us-west1, each rehydrate taking ~120-600ms serially
- 09:17 (Priya): threadpool queues are pegged, new streaming connects are stuck - trying emergency flag toggle walkthrough
- 09:20 (Liam): adjusted LB weights, still seeing 5xx until flag flips
- 09:23 (Aisha): flipped rehydrate_async_mode on cluster, background workers spun up, backlog growing but not blocking threads
- 09:30 (Marisol): alert noise down, p95 trending back down to ~200ms

Notes for postmortem review meeting:
- Bring runtime and platform leads to discuss autoscaler canary strategy and placement staggering.
- Validate the safety of async rehydrate under heavy background I/O load (risk: IO saturation on instance).
- Review monitoring retention for per-instance metrics to ensure we can retroactively investigate future incidents.

This document is a draft postmortem and runbook update. Please add comments below and flag any missed technical details; final version will be posted to Confluence after review and acceptance by runtime, platform, and SRE leads.
